event: On power-up after 1 to 2 months of storage, SB40X VXE376 with its own avionics showed no PWM to the forward motor ESC, a corrupted XCOMM event log, a missing XCOMM config and an uncommanded reset on the ground; the avionics were swapped and red tagged.
component: 376 avionics enclosure (XCOMM and its SD card)
failure_mode: corrupted XCOMM event log data, XCOMM config not retrievable, slow or blank web pages
contributing: 1 to 2 months of storage before power-up
uncommanded reset explained as a known reset-resend behavior

evidence.quote: After reviewing xcomm event log, data appeared to be corrupted. SD card was replaced from older style to updated industrial SD.
A soft reset was performed and ~1min later aircraft reset uncommanded. Due to this, avionics was swapped for alternate set and 376 avionics red tagged.
Due to discovery on 695 avionics (VXEP-1307), this avionics should be inspected for any power issues, consistent with any findings from https://jenaero.atlassian.net/browse/XKIT-4730  investigation.
Hardware related to 695, 376 placed in storage under stairwell in NCR/red tagged cabinet.

would_settle_it.what: power supply to XCOMM and network switch, SD socket and XCOMM board condition
fuel cell or grounding findings from the related 376/695 network troubleshooting

reasoning: The ticket only records symptoms on the 376 avionics (corrupted XCOMM log, missing config, slow web pages) and that the avionics were swapped and red tagged. The planned power inspection was never done: the ticket was canceled into XKIT-4741, which was itself canceled as Won't Do, and the hardware went to the NCR cabinet. So the fault is narrowed to the 376 avionics set, with no part named.
notes: Ticket canceled and moved to XKIT-4741, which duplicates it word for word and has no findings. VXEP-1307 and XKIT-4730 cover a separate network issue on the same airframe with the 695 avionics installed (fuel cell grounding suspected, not resolved). The uncommanded reset was explained as a known behavior where an unacknowledged reset is resent later.

event: During 6.5 software testing, flight ops could not connect to VXE689 on the ground; the Silvus radio was found dead and replacing it with an asset vehicle radio restored the link.
failure_mode: radio unresponsive (no ping, RX 0 on its XCOMM switch port) although it was warm and powered
contributing: original radio was reinstalled after testing and not fully secured

evidence.quote: Did some additional troubleshooting with Carson (will copy below), but determined that the radio is dead. Replaced it with an asset vehicle radio, and everything was working.
SW2 Port5 link - RX was 0 and TX was jumping between 17-50
Checked radio connectors, both ODU connectors in the nosecone - fully seated
Radio was confirmed inop

would_settle_it.file: teardown of the original 689 Silvus radio
would_settle_it.what: which part inside the radio failed (power input, Ethernet interface)

reasoning: Pinging the radio got nothing and its switch port showed no received traffic, while connectors were seated and the camera and Trillium answered on direct connection. Swapping in an asset vehicle radio restored everything, and the team later confirmed the radio inop. The swap test isolates the Silvus radio, although the failed part inside it is not known.

event: Internal asset VXE-734 declared a lost-link launch abort right after lifting off, made its normal 10 ft aft move, struck the aircraft stand with the front prop and hit the ground with the front left motor.
component: lost-link timeout during launch (system clock or RTC update timing)
failure_mode: lost-link launch abort declared within less than the 5 second timeout, possibly because an RTC clock update shifted the timer
contributing: aft move on abort brought the aircraft into the stand
sys cmd fail errors seen in the logs
link timeouts did not clear for about 122 seconds

evidence.quote: @Jason Scherer There is an RTC update directly before the lost link timeout. Could the system clock be getting updated, resulting in the timeout triggering prematurely?
In this case there doesn’t seem to actually be 5 seconds for this event to be triggered from launch to the abort.
@David Grosher You might be on to something here. The clock updates right before the link drop is declared. The puzzling part is that the link timeouts do not resolve for ~2 minutes (122 seconds).
Closing due to inactivity, its an internal aircraft and has been flying with no other issues.

team_view_in_comments: The clock updates right before the link drop is declared.

would_settle_it.what: link status versus RTC update timing around the abort
XCOMM and FWAP logs of the link timeout and clock update

would_settle_it.file: HIL test of repeated clock updates
would_settle_it.what: whether clock updates trigger a premature lost-link abort, as Jason proposed

reasoning: The abort was a lost-link launch abort, but the engineers noted it fired sooner than the 5 second timeout allows and right after an RTC update, which points at the timeout timing rather than a real radio loss. However the link also stayed bad for about 2 minutes, which a clock jump alone does not explain, and the HIL test was never reported. The cause is narrowed to the vehicle lost-link timing logic with a credible radio link alternative.
notes: Front left motor and front prop were damaged by the ground and stand strike; they are consequences, not the cause, so position is left empty. RMA-720 has no teardown findings. Ticket closed for inactivity.

event: FLOPS asset VXE 491 with a Block 35X prototype center wing (CW 4036) lost all avionics data and all lift motors stopped at once during VTOL descent after transition, and the aircraft crashed and was lost.
component: Main System Harness connector to avionics enclosure (Black Alden)
failure_mode: connector not fully mated after an avionics swap, came un-mated from vibration, removing power from the avionics
contributing: aircraft recently used to test a spare avionics enclosure, requiring un-mate and re-mate of the harness
no assembly quality check on test assets

evidence.quote: Was communicated in person but wanted to write this down for future reference that when taking the avionics box out of the fuselage, the grey debug connector was the only one connected.
No Power anomalies prior to the end of the log.
@Greg Fryer This is a look at where each processor stops logging by correlating VTOL Throttles. All logging stops within 5.22 seconds.
[13:59:02.226 1643.226] host vtol state was, is: APVTOL_TAXILZ APVTOL_DESCENT
[21:58:55.090 4435.090] VTOL State Change (was is):  LAND_WAITLZCMD LAND_DESCENDING

team_root_cause: Aircraft 491 was previously used to flight test a spare Avionics Enclosure, which requires un-mating/remating the Main System Harness, which provides power to the avionics. Data shows loss of power to Avionics during VTOL landing. Further, on inspection of asset, it was noted that the Main System Harness was not connected to the avionics (“Black Alden”). That connection is robust enough, if fully mated, that it is not expected to un-mate, even in a crash. Given the alignment of the physical state and data, the root cause is determined to be incomplete re-assembly, allowing the connector to com

would_settle_it.what: confirm all processors stop logging together
latch and pin witness marks showing partial mating

reasoning: Both the VTOL and XCOMM event logs end abruptly at the start of descent with no warnings, and the next entries are a fresh power-on boot, so the avionics lost power. All processors stopped logging within about 5 seconds with no power anomaly beforehand, and on teardown the black main harness connector to the avionics was found disconnected. The aircraft had just had its avionics swapped, so an incompletely mated connector is the best supported cause, though as the team says it cannot be proven beyond the physical state.
notes: Event logs were read with repetitive TRACE, ISR, gcsif/version and GNSS Query lines skipped; the CSV attachments hold headers only. VTOL log tail number reads VC4036 (the center wing); XCOMM reads 491. FS2-3426 covers battery disposition after the crash (both packs damaged), not the cause. Ryan later corrected that only the black main harness was disconnected (no transponder port on this box).

event: Systemic issue on Block 30 aircraft: the MCM resets (on the ground and in flight) when 28V payloads such as the E140, MWIR or E95 are powered on or cycled, losing the mission plan and forcing contingency behavior.
component: MCM eFuse TPS16630 on SLA Breakout Board V2 (MCM powered from NON_CRITICAL payload bus)
failure_mode: payload plus DC-DC converter inrush, back-fed through the common payload/MCM return, trips the eFuse fast-trip comparator or drops the MCM enable line, resetting the MCM
contributing: high inrush payloads (E140 before interface board, MWIR, E95)
powering several Aux ports at once
Rev H Avbox with decoupling capacitors reduces but may not remove the risk

evidence.quote: we are able to recreate the MCM resetting when power cycling the E140
When the E140 is installed there is a shift in relative GND for the 3.3V signal that enables the MCM. Granted this didn't always guarantee that the enable line would drop.
- Risk exists when powering on 28V payloads. The payload power return is common with the MCM on certain avionics boxes.

- SLA Breakout Board V3 2123714-01 Rev A: Added decoupling capacitors. Significantly reduced the likelihood of such an event, but it could still be possible with a lot of payload capacitance/inrush current.
- Records show that this aircraft has 2119959-01-Z rev H avbox, which we thought was not susceptible to this issue. Need to determine if correct, and update containment if so.

team_root_cause:
- Inrush current, on theNON_CRITICAL bus, of E140payload + DC-DC converter​
- Resulting back-fed inrushcurrent tripping the fast-tripcomparator on the TPS16630Efuse (max 45A)

would_settle_it.what: measured inrush current and eFuse trip versus payload configuration

would_settle_it.file: VXEP-1315 MCM Reset on E140 Connection.pptx (SharePoint)
would_settle_it.what: scope captures separating eFuse trip from enable-line ground shift

reasoning: Engineering recreated the MCM reset on the bench by power cycling the E140, both from software and by unplugging, and scoped a ground shift on the MCM enable line. The team root cause names inrush on the NON_CRITICAL bus tripping the TPS16630 eFuse, and the fix history (moving MCM to the critical bus on B40, decoupling capacitors on Breakout V3) is consistent with that. Confidence is medium because the scope data also shows an enable-line ground shift mechanism, and a reset on a Rev H box (PLD-237) is still open.
notes: Umbrella ticket covering many incidents (VXEP-1890, VXEP-1956, VXEP-2005, VXEP-2003, VXEP-844 and others in the incidents table); no single tail. PLD-29 was moved into this ticket. Team root cause text has missing spaces in the export.

event: Standard VXE30 aircraft V666 and V551 in FLOPS had XCOMM watchdog reset boot loops on 6/26/25 while on firmware 6.4, with E140 gimbals fitted.
component: GCS imager message relayed by FWAP to XCOMM
failure_mode: GCS sends a corrupted imager message; FWAP holds and keeps resending it, and XCOMM watchdog-resets each time it tries to send the status response to console debug
contributing: vehicle firmware 6.4 lacked the message validation added in 6.5
conductive gimbal plate shared between gimbals (judged unrelated)

evidence.quote: Dave was just asking me about a previous XComm WDT reset which he said was excatly the same to the one we fixed in 6.5
Ok then this may be a known bug that we fixed already in 6.5
The 551 was on 6.5 GCS. and 666 was on 6.4 GCS
- Validate the message contents on FW AP and XCOMM [COMPLETE in v6.5]

team_root_cause: GCS sends corrupted imager message to XCOMM → FW AP → XCOMM. Because the FW AP holds the value it continues to send it to the XCOMM resulting in the boot loop cycle when the XCOMM tries to send the status response to the console debug. Note: this can be caused with CTRL+F prior to establishing a vehicle connection on v6.4.

would_settle_it.file: V666 and V551 XCOMM event logs
would_settle_it.what: repeating WDT resets at the status response to console debug
conductive plate follow-up, to rule out the E140 hardware path

reasoning: The chat shows both aircraft were on 6.4 vehicle firmware and that the reset matched a known XCOMM WDT bug fixed in 6.5, and the corrective action records message validation on FWAP and XCOMM completed in 6.5. The mechanism (corrupted GCS imager message looping through FWAP to XCOMM) is stated by the team but no log is attached here, so it is narrowed rather than proven. The failure starts in the GCS message, with the older vehicle firmware allowing it to become a boot loop.
notes: Two aircraft on one ticket (666 on 6.4 GCS, 551 on 6.5 GCS). Separated from the MCM reset chat of VXEP-1315; Dave stated it is not E140 related.

event: On a flight test of VXE 674, fuel cell D4599988 ran at maximum temperature in the red and did not cool, so the aircraft landed early; the fuel cell then showed a shutdown error.
failure_mode: fuel cell over-temperature indication, did not report shutdown

evidence.quote: As soon as it got to temp, it stayed maxed out on the temp gauge in the red. It did not indicate any cooling to the Green or yellow so we landed asap to prevent any damage.
Temp cooled when we shut down the fuel cell, but we had an error and it never indicated that it had shut down.
@Sean Wendling Have you had a chance to look at this?

would_settle_it.what: fuel cell temperature, power and state at the time of the over-temperature
fuel cell temperature sensor versus stack power and fan or cooling state
cooling path blockage, fan, or temperature sensor fault

It is not known whether the stack actually overheated, the cooling failed or the temperature sensor read wrong. The evidence does not get past the symptom.

event: During the second flight of the day, VXE 734 arrived over the planned landing zone with lift motors engaged and drifted well past it before touching down; the aircraft was grounded.
component: manual nudge (U-Drive) mode during VTOL landing
failure_mode: autopilot placed in manual nudge mode during landing, then non-zero pitch and roll nudge commands drove the drift
contributing: U-Drive activated about 2 minutes after the RTB command

evidence.quote: @Drew Hildreth I took a look through the logs.  It looks like when the drift occured, the autopilot was in ‘manual nudge’ mode, and the nudge commands were 0.
In the event log 2 minutes after the RTB command you see the U-Drive Activated, and then 1 minute later we see the pause commands
- **Issue Status:** Likely operator error: accidental enabling of manual nudge.

team_view_in_comments: Likely operator error: accidental enabling of manual nudge.

would_settle_it.what: manual nudge mode and nudge command timeline during the drift
GCS event log of who activated U-Drive and when

reasoning: The autopilot log shows manual nudge mode active from about time 1390 with zero commands, then non-zero pitch and roll nudge commands from about 1422 when the drift occurred, and the event log shows U-Drive activated after RTB. The team concluded accidental enabling of manual nudge by the operator. The crew did not confirm doing so, so confidence is medium.
notes: The mishap form attachment converted only as the blank template text, with no operator statements. The team conclusion is in the Issue Status field and comments, not a Root Cause field.
